questions.q: According to the DSM-5-TR criteria taught in this module, what is the minimum requirement to diagnose major depressive disorder?
ch: At least 2 of 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks plus a confirmatory serum marker
Any 3 of the 9 symptoms present for at least 1 week, regardless of impairment
At least 5 of 9 symptoms lasting at least 6 months, including guilt or worthlessness
At least 5 of 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, including depressed mood or anhedonia, with functional impairment
All 9 of the 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, with psychomotor change mandatory
questions.exp: DSM-5-TR requires at least 5 of 9 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, at least one of which must be depressed mood or anhedonia, causing functional impairment.
why: Two symptoms is below threshold, and the module stresses there is no confirmatory lab test for MDD.
Three symptoms over one week falls short of both the symptom count and the two-week duration, and functional impairment is required.
Six months is the duration threshold used for generalized anxiety disorder; MDD requires only two weeks.
All nine symptoms are not required — five suffice — and no single symptom such as psychomotor change is mandatory.

questions.q: The mnemonic SIG E CAPS is taught for major depressive disorder. Which set of items does it represent?
ch: Distractibility, Impulsivity, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, decreased Sleep need, Talkativeness
Restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, and confabulation
Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms
Sleep change, Interest loss, Guilt, Energy loss, Concentration impairment, Appetite change, Psychomotor change, Suicidal ideation
questions.exp: SIG E CAPS — Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidality — plus depressed mood is the module's memory aid for the nine MDD criteria.
why: That list is DIG FAST, the mnemonic the app uses for manic symptoms in bipolar disorder.
Those are the associated symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder, not the MDD criteria.
That describes the Wernicke/Korsakoff picture taught under alcohol withdrawal, not depression.
Those are the five core DSM-5 symptom domains used to diagnose schizophrenia.

questions.q: The module highlights a black-box warning attached to antidepressants. Which group does it identify as requiring especially close early monitoring?
ch: Pregnant patients in the third trimester
Patients with comorbid chronic pain
Patients under 25 years of age
Patients with a first-degree relative who has depression
Patients over 65 years of age
questions.exp: The black-box suicidality warning applies to patients under 25, and the module pairs it with close monitoring early in therapy.
why: Peripartum depression is listed as a specifier and brexanolone/zuranolone as options, but pregnancy is not the black-box group.
Comorbid pain steers drug choice toward an SNRI such as duloxetine; it is not the black-box population.
Heritability is roughly 40%, but family history is not what the black-box warning is keyed to.
Older adults carry other cautions such as TCA and anticholinergic risk, but the black-box suicidality warning is specified for those under 25.

questions.q: A patient with major depression reports prominent insomnia and a 12-pound unintentional weight loss. Which agent does the module specifically match to this presentation?
ch: Phenelzine
Nortriptyline
Fluoxetine
Bupropion
Mirtazapine
questions.exp: The module matches insomnia with poor appetite and weight loss to mirtazapine, whose sedation and weight gain become therapeutic rather than unwanted effects.
why: Phenelzine is an MAOI reserved for atypical or treatment-resistant depression and requires a tyramine-free diet.
Nortriptyline is a TCA used second- or third-line for refractory or melancholic depression and is lethal in overdose.
Fluoxetine is a first-line SSRI, but it is not the agent the module matches to insomnia with weight loss.
Bupropion is reserved for depression with fatigue or low energy, or when sexual and weight side effects must be avoided; it is activating and would worsen insomnia.

questions.q: A nurse cares for a severely depressed patient started on sertraline 10 days ago. The patient is noticeably more energetic and active but still voices hopelessness. What does the module teach about this?
ch: It is an anticholinergic effect that will fade without any change in monitoring
Psychomotor retardation can lift before mood improves, so suicide risk may rise and precautions must continue
It confirms a full therapeutic response, so the dose can now be reduced
It signals serotonin syndrome and the SSRI should be stopped at once
It indicates an antidepressant-induced manic switch requiring a mood stabilizer
questions.exp: The module warns of a paradoxical energy surge in the first 1-2 weeks of antidepressant therapy: as psychomotor retardation lifts before mood improves, suicide risk can rise.
why: Anticholinergic effects belong to the TCAs, and this change demands more monitoring rather than less.
Full antidepressant effect takes 2-6 weeks, and persisting hopelessness shows the mood symptoms have not yet responded.
Serotonin syndrome presents with agitation, tremor, fever and clonus, not with isolated improvement in activity.
A manic switch involves elevated or irritable mood with decreased need for sleep and grandiosity, not persisting hopelessness.

questions.q: How does the module define treatment-resistant depression?
ch: A PHQ-9 score that remains above 20 at the first follow-up visit
Failure of at least two adequate antidepressant trials, meaning adequate dose and duration
Any relapse occurring after the medication has been tapered and stopped
Failure of a single antidepressant given for two weeks at any dose
Failure of psychotherapy alone after six months of weekly sessions
questions.exp: Treatment-resistant depression is failure of at least two adequate antidepressant trials — adequate dose and duration, which the module defines as a therapeutic dose for 6-8 weeks — and prompts augmentation, ECT, or esketamine.
why: A high PHQ-9 grades severity and guides titration, but resistance is defined by failed drug trials.
Relapse after taper is why maintenance runs 6-12 months or longer; it is not the definition of resistance.
Two weeks is far short of an adequate trial; the module defines adequacy as a therapeutic dose for 6-8 weeks.
The definition is anchored on failed antidepressant trials, not on the number of psychotherapy sessions.

questions.q: Which statement about ECT best reflects the module's teaching?
ch: It is the most effective acute treatment and is indicated for severe or psychotic depression, catatonia, acute suicidality, and pregnancy
It is a true last resort, permitted only after both esketamine and an MAOI trial have clearly failed
It is contraindicated during pregnancy because of the risk of inducing fetal seizures and preterm labor
It is used mainly for mild depression that has not responded to a course of psychotherapy alone
It works by directly raising synaptic serotonin faster than any SSRI can achieve
questions.exp: The module calls ECT the fastest and most effective acute treatment — explicitly not a last resort — with indications including severe or psychotic depression, catatonia, acute suicidality, pregnancy, and refractory illness.
why: The module states plainly that ECT is not a last resort; it is the fastest and most effective option for severe disease.
Pregnancy is listed as an indication for ECT in this module, not as a contraindication.
ECT is reserved for severe, psychotic, catatonic, suicidal, or refractory depression rather than mild illness.
ECT's benefit is not explained by an immediate rise in synaptic serotonin; the module ties therapeutic lag to downstream neuroplasticity and BDNF.

questions.q: Three weeks after starting an SSRI for what was diagnosed as major depression, a 22-year-old is sleeping 3 hours a night, speaking rapidly, and has spent his tuition money. What does the module direct?
ch: Emergence of mania or hypomania — reassess for bipolar disorder and stop the offending agent
This is a discontinuation syndrome; restart the SSRI at the original dose and taper slowly
This is akathisia from the SSRI; add a beta-blocker and continue at the current dose
This is the expected paradoxical energy surge; continue the SSRI and reassess in two weeks
This is serotonin syndrome; add cyproheptadine and continue the SSRI at a lower dose
questions.exp: The module lists emergence of mania or hypomania after starting an antidepressant as a red flag: reassess for bipolar disorder and stop the offending agent, since unopposed antidepressant can precipitate mania or rapid cycling.
why: Discontinuation syndrome follows abrupt stopping of the drug, and this patient is still taking it.
Akathisia is a motor restlessness, not reduced sleep need with pressured speech and impulsive spending.
The paradoxical energy surge is a lift in psychomotor retardation during the first 1-2 weeks, not decreased sleep need with grandiose spending.
Serotonin syndrome is agitation, tremor, fever and clonus, not a sustained elevated-mood syndrome.

questions.q: A patient who frequently misses doses asks which antidepressant is least likely to cause symptoms if a dose is skipped. Which answer matches the module's pearls?
ch: Venlafaxine, because it has both serotonergic and noradrenergic activity
Amitriptyline, because its anticholinergic effects buffer withdrawal symptoms
Phenelzine, because monoamine oxidase inhibition is irreversible
Fluoxetine, because its long half-life makes it effectively self-tapering
Paroxetine, because it is highly protein-bound in plasma
questions.exp: The module's pearl is that fluoxetine has the longest half-life and is therefore self-tapering, while paroxetine and venlafaxine have the worst discontinuation syndrome.
why: Venlafaxine is specifically cited for a marked discontinuation syndrome, and the module also warns it raises blood pressure.
Amitriptyline is a TCA reserved for refractory or melancholic depression and is lethal in overdose; the module does not present it as forgiving of missed doses.
Phenelzine is an MAOI requiring a tyramine-free diet and washout periods, which makes erratic adherence more dangerous rather than safer.
Paroxetine is named as one of the two agents with the worst discontinuation syndrome.

questions.q: A patient describes hypersomnia, marked overeating, a heavy leaden feeling in the limbs, and intense sensitivity to perceived rejection. Which specifier and drug class does the module attach to this picture?
ch: Peripartum depression — consider brexanolone or zuranolone
Melancholic depression — consider esketamine under REMS monitoring
Atypical depression — consider an MAOI such as phenelzine
Psychotic depression — consider antipsychotic augmentation or ECT
Seasonal depression — consider bupropion for its activating profile
questions.exp: Atypical depression is defined in the module as hypersomnia, hyperphagia, leaden paralysis and rejection sensitivity, and MAOIs are the class it lists for atypical or treatment-resistant disease.
why: Brexanolone and zuranolone are named for postpartum depression, which is not the presentation described here.
Melancholic features are a separate specifier, and esketamine is reserved for treatment-resistant depression and acute suicidality.
Psychotic features mean delusions or hallucinations such as nihilistic guilt or command content, which this patient does not have.
Seasonal is a listed specifier, but the described cluster of leaden paralysis and rejection sensitivity defines atypical depression.

questions.q: Per the module, generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry lasting how long, plus how many associated symptoms?
ch: At least 6 months of worry plus at least 3 associated symptoms
At least 2 weeks of worry plus at least 4 associated symptoms
At least 6 weeks of worry plus at least 2 associated symptoms
At least 12 months of worry plus at least 6 associated symptoms
At least 1 month of worry plus at least 5 associated symptoms
questions.exp: GAD is defined as excessive worry for at least 6 months plus at least 3 of restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance.
why: Two weeks is the duration threshold for a major depressive episode, not for GAD.
The module specifies six months, not six weeks, along with three associated symptoms.
Twelve months and six symptoms overstate both thresholds the module gives.
One month of anticipatory worry is the panic disorder criterion, and GAD requires three associated symptoms rather than five.

questions.q: Which screening tool and cut-off does the module use to quantify anxiety severity?
ch: PHQ-9, with a score of 15 or more indicating moderate anxiety
CIWA-Ar, with a score of 10 or more indicating moderate anxiety
MDQ, with 7 or more positive items indicating moderate anxiety
C-SSRS, with any positive item indicating moderate anxiety
GAD-7, with a score of 10 or more indicating moderate anxiety
questions.exp: The module quantifies anxiety with the GAD-7 and cites 10 or more as moderate — a common threshold at which to consider treatment.
why: PHQ-9 is used alongside the GAD-7, but it screens for comorbid depression rather than grading anxiety severity.
CIWA-Ar grades alcohol withdrawal severity, not anxiety disorders.
The Mood Disorder Questionnaire is a bipolar screening tool.
The C-SSRS is a structured suicide risk assessment instrument, not an anxiety severity scale.

questions.q: A patient with GAD asks whether buspirone can be taken only when she feels panicky. What does the module teach?
ch: It should be reserved for performance anxiety and taken one hour before the event
It can be used as needed, but only if an SSRI is taken at the same time
It must be taken daily, has a delayed onset over weeks, and gives no acute panic relief
It works within 20 minutes and is the preferred rescue agent for panic attacks
It is habit-forming, so it should be limited to occasional use during severe episodes
questions.exp: Buspirone has a delayed onset of weeks, is not effective as a PRN, and gives no acute panic relief — though it is non-sedating and carries no dependence risk.
why: Propranolol, not buspirone, is the agent the module lists for performance or situational anxiety.
Buspirone is listed as a non-sedating augmentation or alternative for GAD, but pairing it with an SSRI does not make it work as needed.
Buspirone's onset is weeks, not minutes, and the module explicitly says it is not effective for acute panic.
The module states buspirone carries no dependence risk; that concern belongs to the benzodiazepines.

questions.q: A patient started on escitalopram for panic disorder calls on day 6 saying her anxiety is worse than before. Which response reflects the module's teaching?
ch: Add a long-term daily benzodiazepine as definitive therapy in place of the SSRI
Stop the drug immediately, because worsening anxiety indicates an allergic reaction
Conclude the diagnosis is wrong and screen her for hyperthyroidism instead
SSRIs can transiently worsen anxiety in the first 1-2 weeks; reinforce adherence while awaiting the 4-6 week effect
Double the dose today, because the starting dose was clearly too low for panic disorder
questions.exp: The module warns that SSRIs may transiently worsen anxiety in the first 1-2 weeks — start low and go slow, and warn patients or they quit early — with full effect at 4-6 weeks.
why: Benzodiazepines are a short-term bridge only and are never definitive long-term monotherapy.
Early worsening is an expected transient effect of the drug, not an allergic reaction.
A TSH should be checked at baseline to exclude hyperthyroidism, but expected early worsening does not overturn the diagnosis.
The module advises starting low, going slow, and titrating, rather than doubling the dose within the first week.

questions.q: Propranolol is being considered for a musician with performance anxiety. Which comorbidity on the module's list makes this a poor choice?
ch: Mild iron-deficiency anemia
Asthma
Gastroesophageal reflux disease
Well-controlled essential hypertension
A long history of migraine headaches
questions.exp: The module lists asthma, bradycardia, and decompensated heart failure as the settings in which propranolol should be avoided, and notes it treats somatic symptoms rather than cognitive worry.
why: Anemia is not one of the listed contraindications, although the module does stress excluding organic mimics generally.
Reflux is not among the situations in which the module says to avoid propranolol.
Hypertension is not a listed contraindication; the blood-pressure caution in this module attaches to venlafaxine, which raises BP.
Migraine is not among the cautions the module gives for propranolol.

questions.q: A patient is having an acute panic attack in the emergency department. Which nursing approach does the module prioritize?
ch: Encourage the patient to describe the childhood origins of the fear in detail
Have the patient breathe rapidly into a paper bag until the symptoms resolve
Stay with the patient in a calm low-stimulation setting, give short simple directions, and guide slow breathing
Leave the patient alone in a darkened room to prevent overstimulation
Provide detailed written teaching about the fear circuit while symptoms peak
questions.exp: The module directs the nurse to stay with the patient, provide a calm low-stimulation environment, use short simple directions, and guide slow breathing.
why: Exploratory work belongs to CBT and exposure therapy over time, not to the peak of an acute attack.
Rapid breathing into a bag is not the taught intervention; the module teaches guided slow diaphragmatic breathing.
The environment should be low-stimulation, but the module directs the nurse to stay with the patient rather than leave them alone.
The priority is to reduce anxiety to a manageable level before beginning any teaching.

questions.q: A 74-year-old with no psychiatric history develops severe new anxiety with palpitations and sweating. Which red flag from the module applies?
ch: New severe anxiety in an older adult suggests a medical cause — pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroidism, hypoxia, or medication — until proven otherwise
Older adults tolerate benzodiazepines well, so lorazepam is the safest first step here
Anxiety of new onset after age 70 is almost always a prodrome of major depressive disorder
No workup is needed, because anxiety disorders are clinical diagnoses with no confirmatory test
This is expected late-onset GAD; start buspirone and reassess in six weeks
questions.exp: The module flags new severe anxiety in an older adult as a signal to think medical cause — pheochromocytoma, hyperthyroid, hypoxia, medication — until proven otherwise.
why: Benzodiazepines carry sedation, dependence and fall risk and are a Beers-criteria concern in the elderly.
Comorbid depression should be screened for, but the module attributes new severe late-onset anxiety to medical causes first.
Anxiety is a clinical diagnosis, yet the module still requires excluding organic mimics such as hyperthyroidism before committing to it.
Anchoring on a primary anxiety disorder is exactly what this red flag warns against, and buspirone's delayed onset would leave a medical cause untreated.

questions.q: Which combination does the module single out as producing dangerous respiratory depression?
ch: CBT plus an SNRI
A benzodiazepine plus opioids or alcohol
Venlafaxine plus hydroxyzine
Buspirone plus hydroxyzine
Propranolol plus an SSRI
questions.exp: The module warns that benzodiazepines combined with opioids or alcohol cause dangerous respiratory depression, and notes benzodiazepines are also a Beers-list concern in the elderly.
why: CBT combined with pharmacotherapy is presented as producing the best outcomes, not as a hazard.
Venlafaxine with hydroxyzine is not the flagged pair; the venlafaxine caution in this module is a dose-related rise in blood pressure.
Buspirone is non-sedating with no dependence risk and hydroxyzine is offered as a non-addictive option; this pair is not the flagged danger.
Propranolol with an SSRI is not the flagged combination; propranolol's cautions are asthma, bradycardia, and decompensated heart failure.

questions.q: A 58-year-old smoker presents with 20 minutes of chest pain, dyspnea, and a sense of dread that peaked within minutes. Which approach matches the module's teaching?
ch: Give a benzodiazepine and discharge once the patient feels calmer, with no further testing
Order a GAD-7 and treat if the score is 10 or more, deferring any cardiac evaluation
Start an SSRI immediately, because chest pain from panic responds within 48 hours
Exclude ACS, PE, and hyperthyroid storm before attributing the episode to a panic attack
Diagnose panic disorder now, since symptoms peaking within minutes are pathognomonic
questions.exp: The module's red flag is explicit: with chest pain, syncope, or arrhythmia, exclude ACS, PE, and hyperthyroid storm before calling it panic — and its workup includes ECG and troponin when chest pain is present.
why: Discharging without evaluation ignores the red flag to exclude ACS and PE first.
The GAD-7 quantifies anxiety severity; it cannot exclude an acute coronary syndrome.
SSRIs take 4-6 weeks for full effect and can transiently worsen anxiety, and starting one does not address a possible ACS.
Peaking within minutes is characteristic of panic, but it is not enough to skip the cardiac and pulmonary workup in this patient.

questions.q: An inpatient develops tremor, tachycardia, and severe anxiety two days after admission. Which module red flag should be considered before treating this as an anxiety disorder?
ch: Serotonin syndrome caused by as-needed hydroxyzine doses
A conversion reaction to the stress of being hospitalized
An emerging manic episode caused by an antidepressant switch
Tardive dyskinesia from a previously prescribed antipsychotic
Benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal masquerading as anxiety
questions.exp: The module lists signs of benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal — tremor, tachycardia, seizures — as a red flag that can masquerade as anxiety, and its workup includes screening for substance withdrawal.
why: Hydroxyzine is an antihistamine, and serotonin syndrome features clonus, fever and agitation rather than this withdrawal timeline.
The module directs excluding substance withdrawal and organic mimics before attributing new symptoms to psychological stress.
A manic switch presents with elevated mood and decreased need for sleep rather than isolated tremor and tachycardia.
Tardive dyskinesia is a late choreoathetoid movement disorder, not an acute autonomic surge.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes bipolar I from bipolar II as the module defines them?
ch: Bipolar I requires both a manic and a major depressive episode, whereas bipolar II requires neither of them
Bipolar I requires a hypomanic episode, while bipolar II requires at least one full manic episode
Bipolar I is diagnosed only after four or more distinct mood episodes have occurred within one year
Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode; bipolar II requires a hypomanic episode plus a major depressive episode with no full mania
Bipolar I and bipolar II differ only in whether psychotic features have ever been present
questions.exp: One manic episode — 7 days or more, or requiring hospitalization — makes it bipolar I, and depression is not required. Bipolar II is a hypomanic episode plus a major depressive episode with no full mania.
why: Depression is common in bipolar I but is not required; a single manic episode is sufficient.
This reverses the definitions: mania defines bipolar I and hypomania defines bipolar II.
Four or more episodes in a year defines rapid cycling, which is a course specifier rather than the type.
Psychosis marks an episode as manic rather than hypomanic, but the type rests on mania versus hypomania, not on psychosis alone.

questions.q: The mnemonic DIG FAST is used for which set of findings?
ch: The laboratory parameters required for monitoring before and during lithium therapy
The five core symptom domains used to diagnose schizophrenia
The nine DSM-5-TR criteria for a major depressive episode
Manic symptoms: distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, increased activity, decreased sleep need, talkativeness
The staged timeline of alcohol withdrawal from tremor through delirium tremens
questions.exp: DIG FAST — Distractibility, Impulsivity/Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity/energy increase, decreased Sleep need, Talkativeness — is the module's mania mnemonic.
why: Lithium monitoring covers level, renal function, TSH and calcium, which is not what DIG FAST stands for.
The schizophrenia criteria are delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms.
SIG E CAPS, not DIG FAST, is the mnemonic for the depressive criteria.
The alcohol withdrawal timeline is tracked by hours from the last drink and graded with CIWA-Ar, not by DIG FAST.

questions.q: Which agent does the module identify as the only mood stabilizer with robust evidence of reducing suicide?
ch: Lithium
Valproate
Lamotrigine
Carbamazepine
Quetiapine
questions.exp: Lithium is the gold-standard mood stabilizer for acute mania and maintenance and has the strongest anti-suicide evidence of any agent in the module.
why: Valproate treats acute mania, mixed episodes and rapid cycling, but the anti-suicide evidence belongs to lithium.
Lamotrigine is used for maintenance and bipolar depression prophylaxis and is weak for acute mania.
Carbamazepine is an alternative for mania, especially mixed or rapid cycling, and is notable for CYP3A4 autoinduction.
Quetiapine covers acute mania, agitation, psychosis and bipolar depression, but lithium is the agent named for suicide reduction.

questions.q: A patient stable on lithium develops coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion after a week of gastroenteritis and daily ibuprofen. Which explanation does the module give?
ch: Ibuprofen displaces lithium from plasma protein binding sites, increasing the free drug fraction
Gastroenteritis induces hepatic CYP3A4 and accelerates the metabolism of lithium
These are expected steady-state effects of a therapeutic lithium level of 0.6-1.2 mEq/L
This is a Stevens-Johnson prodrome, so the lithium must be titrated more slowly
Volume depletion and NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance, raising the level into the toxic range
questions.exp: Lithium is renally cleared, so dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides and ACE inhibitors/ARBs raise levels toward toxicity; coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion are the module's toxicity signs.
why: The module explains lithium toxicity through reduced renal clearance, not through protein-binding displacement.
CYP3A4 autoinduction is a carbamazepine issue; lithium is cleared renally in the module's account.
Tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion are toxicity signs, not expected effects at a therapeutic level.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and slow titration belong to lamotrigine, not to lithium.

questions.q: A hyperactive manic patient will not sit down for meals. Which nursing intervention does the module specify?
ch: Withhold food until the patient agrees to remain seated at the table
Provide a large hot meal in the busy dayroom to encourage social interaction
Offer high-calorie finger foods the patient can eat while moving
Insert a nasogastric tube to guarantee caloric intake during the episode
Restrict fluids to reduce the pacing and agitation before offering any food
questions.exp: The module directs offering high-calorie finger foods the patient can eat on the move, since manic patients may not sit to eat, while promoting rest, hydration and nutrition.
why: Withholding food is punitive and conflicts with the directive to promote nutrition; limits are set on intrusive behavior, not on meals.
A stimulating dayroom setting works against the low-stimulation environment the module requires.
Nothing in the module escalates to tube feeding for a manic patient who is simply too active to sit down.
Hydration is to be promoted, and steady salt and fluid intake is specifically important on lithium.

questions.q: A patient two weeks into a lamotrigine titration reports a spreading rash with mouth sores. What does the module direct?
ch: Stop lamotrigine immediately — this may be Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Hold the lithium and check a lithium level along with renal function
Check an ANC urgently, because this presentation suggests agranulocytosis
Reduce the dose by half and re-titrate back up over the next 48 hours
Continue lamotrigine and add an antihistamine, since rash is common and self-limited
questions.exp: An emerging rash on lamotrigine, especially with mucosal involvement, means stopping the drug immediately for possible Stevens-Johnson syndrome; slow titration is the safeguard against it.
why: Lithium toxicity presents with tremor, ataxia, vomiting and confusion; this patient's problem is a drug rash.
Agranulocytosis with ANC monitoring is a carbamazepine and clozapine concern, not the lamotrigine rash pathway.
Slow titration prevents the reaction, but once rash with mucosal involvement appears the drug is stopped, not re-titrated.
The module treats a rash on lamotrigine as a stop signal, not as a nuisance to manage with antihistamines.

questions.q: A 24-year-old with bipolar II presents in a depressive episode. Why does the module caution against starting an SSRI alone, and what does it favor instead?
ch: SSRIs cause tardive dyskinesia in bipolar patients, so a VMAT2 inhibitor is started first
SSRIs are ineffective in any form of depression, so lamotrigine is used purely as a placebo-sparing measure
SSRIs cause Ebstein anomaly, so valproate is preferred in anyone of childbearing potential
SSRIs raise lithium levels, so carbamazepine must be substituted before any antidepressant is added
Unopposed antidepressants risk a manic switch or rapid cycling, so mood stabilizers or quetiapine, lurasidone or cariprazine come first
questions.exp: The module's antidepressant monotherapy caution: in bipolar depression, unopposed antidepressants risk a manic switch or rapid cycling, so guidelines favor mood stabilizers or quetiapine, lurasidone, or cariprazine — the agents FDA-approved for bipolar depression.
why: Tardive dyskinesia is an antipsychotic complication and VMAT2 inhibitors are its treatment, not a bipolar depression therapy.
The concern is a manic switch rather than lack of antidepressant efficacy, and lamotrigine has real value in preventing depressive relapse.
Ebstein anomaly is the lithium teratogenicity risk, and valproate is the agent to avoid in people who may become pregnant.
Lithium levels rise with dehydration, NSAIDs, thiazides and ACEi/ARBs, not with SSRIs.

questions.q: A 27-year-old with bipolar I is planning a pregnancy. Which pairing of drug and reproductive risk matches the module?
ch: Quetiapine — neural tube defects; valproate — Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Valproate — neural tube defects; lithium — Ebstein anomaly
Lithium — neural tube defects; valproate — Ebstein anomaly
Lamotrigine — Ebstein anomaly; quetiapine — neural tube defects
Carbamazepine — Ebstein anomaly; lithium — agranulocytosis
questions.exp: The module pairs valproate with neural tube defects — avoid it in people who may become pregnant — and lithium with Ebstein anomaly, and notes ECT is an option during pregnancy.
why: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is the lamotrigine and carbamazepine risk; valproate's teratogenic signature is neural tube defects.
This reverses the two: neural tube defects belong to valproate and Ebstein anomaly to lithium.
Lamotrigine's signature risk is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and quetiapine's is metabolic burden.
Ebstein anomaly is a lithium risk, and agranulocytosis is associated with carbamazepine rather than lithium.

questions.q: Which depressive presentation should most strongly prompt screening for bipolar disorder before an antidepressant is started, per the module?
ch: A single mild episode following a job loss, with a normal TSH
Early-onset, recurrent, psychotic or postpartum depression, or prior antidepressant-induced hypomania
Depression with hypersomnia and hyperphagia in a patient over 65
Depression accompanied by muscle tension and six months of uncontrollable worry
A first episode at age 58 with prominent comorbid neuropathic pain
questions.exp: The module says to suspect bipolar in depression that is early-onset, recurrent, psychotic, postpartum, or accompanied by antidepressant-induced hypomania, and notes peak onset is the late teens to mid-20s.
why: A single mild reactive episode with normal thyroid function is not among the bipolar warning features listed.
Hypersomnia and hyperphagia describe atypical depression, for which MAOIs are considered.
Muscle tension with six months of worry describes generalized anxiety disorder.
A later first onset with comorbid pain points toward an SNRI such as duloxetine rather than toward a bipolar screen.

questions.q: A patient with delirious mania is dehydrated, exhausted, and not responding to a mood stabilizer plus an antipsychotic. Per the module, what should be considered?
ch: Discharging with mood charting and close outpatient follow-up
Withholding all fluids to avoid raising the lithium level further
Electroconvulsive therapy — indicated for severe, refractory, or life-threatening mania
Starting an SSRI to address the underlying depressive substrate
Adding lamotrigine and titrating rapidly to a therapeutic dose
questions.exp: Delirious or severe mania with dehydration and exhaustion is called a medical emergency that may need ECT; the module lists ECT for severe or refractory mania or depression, catatonia and pregnancy, and calls it first-line when rapid response is needed.
why: This presentation is described as a medical emergency, not a situation for outpatient management.
Dehydration raises lithium levels toward toxicity; the module directs steady salt and fluid intake.
An antidepressant in bipolar disorder risks a manic switch and would worsen an active manic episode.
Lamotrigine is weak for acute mania and requires slow titration to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

questions.q: Which set of durations distinguishes schizophrenia from schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder in the module?
ch: Brief psychotic disorder under 1 week, schizophreniform 1-3 months, schizophrenia 1 year or more
Brief psychotic disorder under 2 weeks, schizophreniform 2-12 weeks, schizophrenia 3 months or more
All three require six months and are distinguished only by whether negative symptoms are present
Duration is irrelevant; the three are separated by whether the hallucinations are auditory
Brief psychotic disorder under 1 month, schizophreniform 1-6 months, schizophrenia 6 months or more of continuous disturbance
questions.exp: The module's duration-based differential is brief psychotic disorder under 1 month, schizophreniform 1-6 months, and schizophrenia 6 months or more of total continuous disturbance including prodrome and residual, with functional decline.
why: The cut-offs are one month and six months, not one week, three months, and a year.
These intervals do not match the module, which requires at least six months of continuous disturbance for schizophrenia.
Duration is precisely what separates the three diagnoses in the module.
The module bases the differential on duration, not on the modality of the hallucinations.

questions.q: How does the module's dopamine hypothesis explain positive versus negative symptoms?
ch: Mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia drives positive symptoms; mesocortical hypodopaminergia drives negative and cognitive symptoms
Both symptom clusters arise from excess serotonin acting at limbic 5-HT2A receptors
Both symptom clusters arise from NMDA receptor overactivity in the prefrontal cortex
Mesolimbic hypodopaminergia drives positive symptoms; mesocortical hyperdopaminergia drives negative symptoms
Nigrostriatal hyperdopaminergia drives positive symptoms; tuberoinfundibular blockade drives negative symptoms
questions.exp: Mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia drives positive symptoms while mesocortical hypodopaminergia drives negative and cognitive symptoms; glutamate (NMDA hypofunction) and serotonin also contribute.
why: 5-HT2A blockade is part of how atypicals work, but serotonin excess is not the module's explanation for the symptom clusters.
The module describes NMDA hypofunction, not NMDA overactivity.
This reverses the model — the mesolimbic pathway is overactive and the mesocortical pathway is underactive.
The nigrostriatal pathway produces EPS and tardive dyskinesia when blocked, and the tuberoinfundibular pathway governs prolactin.

questions.q: When does the module say clozapine should be started?
ch: After failure of at least two adequate antipsychotic trials — treatment-resistant disease
Only after electroconvulsive therapy has been tried and has failed
As soon as any extrapyramidal symptom appears on another antipsychotic
Whenever a patient develops tardive dyskinesia on a first-generation agent
At first presentation, because it is the most effective agent available
questions.exp: Clozapine is the gold standard for treatment-resistant schizophrenia — failure of at least two antipsychotics — and uniquely reduces suicidality, but the module says it is never first-line because agranulocytosis mandates ANC monitoring.
why: The algorithm escalates to clozapine after two failed antipsychotic trials, and ECT is not a prerequisite in this module.
Extrapyramidal symptoms are managed with benztropine or diphenhydramine, or by switching agents, not by moving to clozapine.
Tardive dyskinesia is treated with a VMAT2 inhibitor such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine.
The module states clozapine is never first-line; two adequate trials must fail first.

questions.q: A patient on haloperidol develops fever, lead-pipe rigidity, labile blood pressure, and a markedly elevated CK. What does the module direct?
ch: Diagnose akathisia and reassure the patient that it will resolve on its own
Hold only the next scheduled dose and recheck the CK in 48 hours
Stop the antipsychotic, cool the patient, and give dantrolene or bromocriptine — this is NMS
Continue the haloperidol and add benztropine to treat the rigidity
Diagnose tardive dyskinesia and start valbenazine at the next visit
questions.exp: NMS is lead-pipe rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and elevated CK; the module directs stopping the antipsychotic, cooling, and giving dantrolene or bromocriptine.
why: Akathisia is subjective inner restlessness, not fever with rigidity and a raised CK.
NMS is a red-flag emergency requiring the drug to be stopped and treated now, not observed.
Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, and continuing the antipsychotic in NMS is dangerous.
Tardive dyskinesia is a late choreoathetoid movement disorder without fever or an elevated CK.

questions.q: Which side-effect pairing matches the module's description of second-generation antipsychotics?
ch: Quetiapine — tardive dyskinesia is impossible with it; olanzapine — causes no weight gain
Olanzapine — the worst metabolic offender; risperidone — raises prolactin
Risperidone — requires REMS ANC monitoring; olanzapine — treats tardive dyskinesia
Olanzapine — the highest prolactin elevation; risperidone — the least metabolic burden of any agent
Aripiprazole — agranulocytosis requiring ANC monitoring; quetiapine — Ebstein anomaly
questions.exp: Among the second-generation agents the module names olanzapine as the worst metabolic offender and risperidone as the one that raises prolactin.
why: Tardive dyskinesia remains a risk with antipsychotics, and olanzapine causes substantial weight gain.
REMS ANC monitoring is clozapine's requirement, and tardive dyskinesia is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors.
This reverses the pairing: olanzapine is the metabolic offender and risperidone is the prolactin-raising agent.
ANC monitoring under REMS belongs to clozapine, and Ebstein anomaly is a lithium risk.

questions.q: A patient tells the nurse that voices are speaking to him. Which approach to hallucinations and delusions does the module teach?
ch: Agree with the content to build rapport and reduce the patient's distress
Acknowledge the patient's feelings while presenting reality, without arguing or reinforcing the content
Ignore the statement entirely and redirect only to activities of daily living
Increase environmental stimulation to distract the patient from the voices
Argue firmly with the content until the patient concedes that it is not real
questions.exp: The module says to establish trust in a calm low-stimulation environment and neither argue with nor reinforce delusions and hallucinations — acknowledge feelings while presenting reality. Command hallucinations are additionally a red flag requiring immediate safety intervention.
why: Agreeing reinforces the hallucination or delusion, which the module prohibits.
Supporting ADLs matters, but ignoring the disclosure misses both the therapeutic response and the safety assessment.
The environment should be kept calm and low-stimulation, not made more stimulating.
Arguing with the content is specifically what the module tells the nurse not to do.

questions.q: A 62-year-old with no psychiatric history develops psychosis over two weeks with a low-grade fever and a new focal neurologic deficit. What does the module advise?
ch: Diagnose schizophreniform disorder, since the duration is under six months
Attribute the picture to negative symptoms and begin psychosocial rehabilitation
Start clozapine, because late-onset psychosis is typically treatment-resistant
Think delirium, autoimmune (anti-NMDA) encephalitis, or CNS pathology rather than primary schizophrenia
Diagnose late-onset schizophrenia and start a second-generation antipsychotic
questions.exp: The module flags new psychosis with focal neuro signs, fever, or older age of onset as a signal for delirium, autoimmune (anti-NMDA) encephalitis, or CNS pathology, and directs MRI/CT and EEG when the presentation is atypical.
why: Schizophreniform disorder is still a primary psychotic diagnosis and requires excluding medical and neurologic causes.
Negative symptoms are flat affect, avolition, alogia and anhedonia — they do not explain fever and a focal deficit.
Clozapine follows two failed antipsychotic trials and is never a first move, least of all before CNS pathology is excluded.
Typical onset is the late teens to mid-20s in men and the late 20s in women; this presentation is atypical and demands a workup first.

questions.q: A patient who has been on clozapine for four weeks calls with fever and a sore throat. What is the correct action per the module?
ch: Add benztropine, because these are early extrapyramidal symptoms
Increase the clozapine dose, since psychosis often flares during an infection
Perform an AIMS exam to screen for tardive dyskinesia at the next scheduled visit
Hold the drug and evaluate urgently for agranulocytosis
Reassure the patient and continue clozapine, since this is a common benign viral illness
questions.exp: Fever and sore throat on clozapine is the module's red flag for agranulocytosis, alongside myocarditis: hold the drug and evaluate urgently, and ensure the ANC draws happen on schedule per REMS.
why: Benztropine treats acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, not fever with sore throat.
Raising the dose ignores a potentially fatal hematologic emergency.
The AIMS exam screens for tardive dyskinesia and does nothing to detect neutropenia.
The module treats these symptoms as a red flag, not as something to reassure the patient about.

questions.q: A patient has relapsed three times after stopping oral risperidone. Which intervention does the module recommend, and with what caveat?
ch: Start a VMAT2 inhibitor, which improves adherence by reducing movement side effects
Switch to haloperidol, because first-generation agents have better adherence profiles
A long-acting injectable — but establish tolerability with the oral form first, and missed injections still risk relapse
Add benztropine prophylactically, since EPS is the usual reason patients stop antipsychotics
Stop all antipsychotics and rely on psychosocial rehabilitation and family psychoeducation
questions.exp: Long-acting injectables improve adherence in chronic or relapsing patients with poor oral compliance; the module's caveats are to ensure tolerability with the oral form first and to recognize that missed injections still risk relapse.
why: VMAT2 inhibitors are the FDA-approved treatment for tardive dyskinesia, not an adherence strategy.
First-generation agents carry high EPS and tardive dyskinesia risk; the module's adherence tool is the long-acting injectable.
Benztropine treats acute dystonia and parkinsonism and is not the module's answer to repeated non-adherence.
Stopping medication is described as the most common cause of relapse, and psychosocial care supplements rather than replaces it.

questions.q: Which statement about outcome and prognosis in schizophrenia matches the module?
ch: Suicide is rare in schizophrenia and cardiovascular disease contributes little to mortality
Prominent negative symptoms and insidious onset predict the best long-term outcome
Lower socioeconomic status causes schizophrenia rather than resulting from it
Negative and cognitive symptoms respond best of all symptoms to current antipsychotics
Acute onset, mood symptoms, older onset, female sex and good premorbid function are favorable
questions.exp: The module lists acute onset, mood symptoms, older onset, female sex and good premorbid function as good prognostic factors, while insidious onset and prominent negative symptoms are poor ones.
why: The module cites elevated mortality from cardiovascular disease and a lifetime suicide risk of roughly 5%.
Insidious onset and prominent negative symptoms are named as poor prognostic factors, not good ones.
The module describes downward drift — low socioeconomic status is a consequence of the illness rather than a cause.
Negative and cognitive symptoms respond poorly to current antipsychotics and best predict long-term disability.

questions.q: What neuroadaptation does the module give as the basis for alcohol and sedative-hypnotic withdrawal?
ch: Chronic alcohol potentiates GABA-A and suppresses NMDA/glutamate; withdrawal leaves unopposed glutamatergic excitation plus a noradrenergic surge
Chronic alcohol blocks mu-opioid receptors, and withdrawal releases locus coeruleus inhibition
Chronic alcohol depletes dopamine stores, and withdrawal produces mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia
Chronic alcohol upregulates GABA-A tone, and withdrawal leaves unopposed GABAergic inhibition
Chronic alcohol downregulates NMDA receptors, and withdrawal produces a glutamate deficiency
questions.exp: Chronic alcohol, benzodiazepines and barbiturates potentiate inhibitory GABA-A tone and suppress excitatory NMDA/glutamate tone; abrupt withdrawal leaves unopposed glutamatergic excitation plus an autonomic noradrenergic surge, which is why GABA agonists are the mechanistically correct treatment.
why: Mu-opioid receptors and the locus coeruleus are the module's mechanism for opioid withdrawal, which it explicitly contrasts with alcohol.
Mesolimbic hyperdopaminergia is the schizophrenia model; the module frames alcohol withdrawal around GABA and glutamate.
Withdrawal removes GABA tone rather than leaving it unopposed — the excess is glutamatergic.
Chronic ethanol upregulates NMDA receptors, and withdrawal produces glutamate excitotoxicity rather than deficiency.

questions.q: Per the module's alcohol withdrawal timeline, when do delirium tremens typically occur after the last drink?
ch: 6-12 hours
12-24 hours
12-48 hours
48-96 hours
7-10 days
questions.exp: The module's timeline is tremor and anxiety at 6-12h, alcoholic hallucinosis at 12-24h, withdrawal seizures at 12-48h, and delirium tremens at 48-96h.
why: Six to twelve hours is when tremor and anxiety appear.
Twelve to twenty-four hours is the window for alcoholic hallucinosis with a clear sensorium.
Twelve to forty-eight hours is when withdrawal seizures occur.
The module places DTs at 48-96 hours, well before a week has elapsed.

questions.q: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder arrives hypoglycemic. What does the module require?
ch: Give thiamine only after the glucose has been normal for 24 hours
Give thiamine before or with the dextrose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
Withhold both until an ethanol level and a CIWA-Ar score are available
Give folate instead, since thiamine is needed only once ataxia is present
Give dextrose immediately and add thiamine only if confusion later develops
questions.exp: Thiamine before glucose — always. Giving glucose first can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so thiamine goes before or with dextrose in every alcohol patient.
why: Delaying thiamine leaves the patient exposed during the very period in which glucose is being given.
Hypoglycemia must be corrected promptly, and the thiamine rule applies regardless of the CIWA-Ar score.
Folate is listed among the deficiencies to correct, but it does not substitute for thiamine, and Wernicke is prevented rather than awaited.
Glucose first is exactly the sequence the module warns can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.q: Why does the module prefer symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing over a fixed schedule?
ch: It eliminates the risk of withdrawal seizures without any pharmacologic prophylaxis
It uses less total drug, shortens treatment duration, and produces fewer complications
It removes the need for any further nursing reassessment once the first dose is given
It allows a lower-potency agent to be used, avoiding all risk of respiratory depression
It substitutes for thiamine repletion in patients who are already malnourished
questions.exp: Symptom-triggered dosing guided by CIWA-Ar means less total benzodiazepine, a shorter duration of treatment, and fewer complications than a fixed schedule.
why: The benzodiazepine is itself the seizure prophylaxis; symptom-triggered dosing changes how it is given, not whether it is needed.
Symptom-triggered dosing depends on serial CIWA-Ar reassessment with documentation of the trend.
Respiratory depression and oversedation remain concerns with any benzodiazepine dosing strategy.
Thiamine is a separate mandatory intervention and is not replaced by any benzodiazepine strategy.

questions.q: Which benzodiazepine does the module prefer for a patient in alcohol withdrawal who has cirrhosis, and why?
ch: Midazolam, because it is the only agent that reliably prevents delirium tremens
Chlordiazepoxide, because its long half-life provides an automatic taper
Lorazepam, because it has no active metabolites
Diazepam, because hepatic metabolism is increased in cirrhosis
Phenobarbital, because it is a benzodiazepine with purely hepatic clearance
questions.exp: The module specifies lorazepam in liver failure and in the elderly because it has no active metabolites, while still watching for oversedation and respiratory depression.
why: No single benzodiazepine is described as uniquely preventing DTs; symptom-triggered dosing of a first-line agent does that.
Chlordiazepoxide is a listed first-line agent, but the module names lorazepam specifically for liver failure and the elderly.
Hepatic metabolism is impaired, not increased, in cirrhosis, which is precisely why agents with active metabolites are avoided.
Phenobarbital is a barbiturate rather than a benzodiazepine and is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory or severe withdrawal.

questions.q: A patient in severe withdrawal is started on dexmedetomidine for tachycardia and hypertension. What caution does the module give?
ch: Autonomic adjuncts are contraindicated in withdrawal because they mask the CIWA-Ar score entirely
Dexmedetomidine should replace the benzodiazepines in order to minimize total sedation
Dexmedetomidine treats Wernicke encephalopathy and makes thiamine unnecessary
Clonidine and propranolol are first-line and benzodiazepines are only adjuncts
Adjuncts control autonomic hyperactivity but do not prevent seizures or DTs, so benzodiazepines must continue
questions.exp: Dexmedetomidine, propranolol and clonidine are adjuncts for autonomic hyperactivity only — the module states plainly that they do not replace benzodiazepines because they do not prevent seizures or DTs.
why: The module lists these agents as useful adjuncts rather than contraindicated, while cautioning that they are not seizure prophylaxis.
The module says explicitly that these agents do not replace benzodiazepines.
Wernicke prophylaxis and treatment is high-dose thiamine; no autonomic adjunct substitutes for it.
The ordering is reversed: benzodiazepines are first-line and clonidine or propranolol are the adjuncts.

questions.q: Eighteen hours after his last drink, a man reports seeing bugs on the wall but is fully oriented with normal vital signs. How should this be classified per the module?
ch: Wernicke encephalopathy, given the new visual disturbance
Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis until neuroimaging proves otherwise
Alcoholic hallucinosis — hallucinations with a clear sensorium at roughly 12-24 hours
Delirium tremens, because visual hallucinations are what define DTs
A withdrawal seizure prodrome requiring immediate phenobarbital loading
questions.exp: Alcoholic hallucinosis occurs at roughly 12-24 hours with a clear sensorium, in contrast to delirium tremens at 48-96 hours, which adds clouded consciousness and autonomic instability.
why: Wernicke encephalopathy is confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, and this patient is oriented with normal vital signs.
Autoimmune encephalitis is a consideration for atypical new psychosis, not for a classic withdrawal timeline.
DTs require clouded consciousness and autonomic instability at 48-96 hours, neither of which fits this patient.
Withdrawal seizures fall at 12-48 hours, but this patient has hallucinations with a clear sensorium, and phenobarbital is reserved for refractory or severe withdrawal.

questions.q: Which factor does the module call the strongest predictor that a patient will have a withdrawal seizure or delirium tremens?
ch: A urine drug screen that is positive for opioids
An elevated mean corpuscular volume on the CBC
A first-ever drinking binge lasting more than one week
A high blood alcohol concentration on arrival
A prior history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens
questions.exp: The module names prior DTs or withdrawal seizures as the strongest predictor of recurrence, alongside a high CIWA score, comorbid illness, and older age.
why: Opioid withdrawal is uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening and does not predict DTs.
Mean corpuscular volume is not among the DT predictors the module lists.
The module emphasizes prior withdrawal complications rather than the length of a single first binge.
An ethanol level is part of the lab workup but is not the predictor the module singles out.

questions.q: A patient's CIWA-Ar scores keep climbing despite escalating lorazepam doses. What does the module say refractory withdrawal points toward?
ch: Phenobarbital, or magnesium and electrolyte correction, rather than simply more benzodiazepine
Beginning disulfiram so the patient associates alcohol with illness
Reducing the benzodiazepine dose, because oversedation is masking improvement
Switching to buprenorphine to cover a concurrent opioid withdrawal
Starting naltrexone immediately to blunt the craving driving the agitation
questions.exp: Refractory withdrawal points to phenobarbital or to magnesium and electrolyte correction rather than just more benzodiazepine; escalating benzodiazepine requirements is itself a red flag for impending DT or a missed diagnosis.
why: Disulfiram is a maintenance agent requiring adherence and no recent alcohol, not an acute treatment.
Escalating requirements signal impending DT or a missed diagnosis, so reducing therapy would be dangerous.
Buprenorphine treats opioid withdrawal and can precipitate withdrawal if given too early; it does nothing for alcohol withdrawal.
Naltrexone is for maintaining abstinence after withdrawal is complete and is contraindicated with active opioid use.

questions.q: How does the module characterize opioid withdrawal compared with alcohol withdrawal?
ch: Identical in mechanism, since both act through GABA-A and NMDA receptors
Safely managed with symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar dosing of benzodiazepines
Best treated by withholding all medication so that tolerance resets completely
Intensely uncomfortable but rarely lethal in healthy adults; the danger lies in relapse with lost tolerance
More lethal than alcohol withdrawal because of its seizures and delirium tremens
questions.exp: Opioid withdrawal is intensely uncomfortable — flu-like and GI — but rarely life-threatening in healthy adults; the risk lies in relapse and lost tolerance driving overdose, and it is treated with buprenorphine or methadone plus symptomatic clonidine, ondansetron and loperamide.
why: Opioids act via mu-opioid receptors and the locus coeruleus, which the module explicitly contrasts with the GABA-A/NMDA mechanism.
CIWA-Ar grades alcohol withdrawal; opioid readiness is screened with COWS and treated with buprenorphine or methadone.
Withholding treatment increases suffering and relapse risk; the module urges starting MAT during the admission.
Seizures and delirium tremens belong to alcohol and sedative-hypnotic withdrawal, which the module calls the dangerous, potentially fatal type.
